title: Traveling Salesmen

jokes.text: Michael introduces Harvey the computer, which immediately says 'Jim sucks.'
jokes.setup: Michael calls Jim into his office with an air of importance, suggesting something professional is happening.
jokes.punchline: A computer named Harvey immediately insults Jim — 'Jim sucks' — and Michael feigns helplessness: 'I can't control him.'
jokes.explanation: Works because it captures Michael's childish prank energy perfectly — he clearly programmed Harvey to say this and is delighted by it. Jim's deadpan 'Yeah, you can' is the real punchline. Efficient and character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael says 'Sorry. Zing.' apologizing for Harvey's insult while simultaneously claiming credit for it.
jokes.setup: Harvey insults Jim; Michael acts as though it's out of his control.
jokes.punchline: 'Sorry. Zing.' — Michael can't resist taking credit for his own setup.
jokes.explanation: The two-word 'Sorry. Zing.' is a perfect distillation of Michael's personality — he wants to be both polite and edgy simultaneously. The economy is exceptional. Fully character-specific.

jokes.text: Harvey says 'Pam, you look very hot today' after Michael calls Pam in.
jokes.setup: Michael calls Pam in to meet Harvey, ostensibly for a normal workplace reason.
jokes.punchline: Harvey immediately sexually harasses Pam, which is clearly Michael's doing — extending the bit and revealing Michael's inappropriate feelings.
jokes.explanation: Cringe lands because it's so on-brand for Michael to use a tech toy to say what he can't say himself. A bit predictable as an escalation of the Harvey bit, but the discomfort is genuine.

jokes.text: Harvey says 'Me so horny. Me love you long tim.' to Pam.
jokes.setup: Harvey has already been inappropriate; Michael introduces Pam formally to Harvey.
jokes.punchline: Harvey delivers a racist/sexual movie quote, escalating the discomfort dramatically.
jokes.explanation: The cringe escalation works structurally, but the joke itself relies on an old pop-culture reference with a racial dimension that makes it uncomfortable in a non-comedically rewarding way. The craft is mediocre; the impact comes from shock value.

jokes.text: Michael mishears 'long time' as a person's name: 'Who is Long Tim?'
jokes.setup: Harvey says 'Me love you long time' — a well-known phrase.
jokes.punchline: Michael, revealing his complete cultural obliviousness, thinks 'Long Tim' is a person and asks who he is.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely sharp character joke. Michael's obliviousness isn't just stupid — it reveals he set up the bit without fully understanding it. The deadpan earnestness of 'Who is Long Tim?' is pitch-perfect Michael Scott. Strong character integration; only Michael would be this confidently clueless.

jokes.text: After Jim explains 'long time,' Michael says 'Oh, well, you should bring Long Tim in one day. I'd love to meet Long Tim.'
jokes.setup: Jim corrects Michael — it's 'long time,' not a person.
jokes.punchline: Michael doesn't absorb the correction and doubles down, still treating Long Tim as a real person.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first genuinely excellent joke. The structure is impeccable: correction → failure to absorb → escalation. Michael inviting 'Long Tim' in is a perfect character moment — his obliviousness isn't passive, it's active and enthusiastic. 'I'd love to meet Long Tim' has quotability and rewatch value. The escalation from mishearing to genuinely wanting to socialize with the fictional person is inspired.

jokes.text: Jim tells Michael 'You ruined a funny joke' and Michael responds 'You get out of my off-five.'
jokes.setup: Jim correctly points out Michael ruined his own joke by not understanding it.
jokes.punchline: Michael tries to say 'Get out of my office' but says 'off-five' — an accidental portmanteau, possibly referencing 'high five' — delivered with full authority.
jokes.explanation: A decent malapropism from Michael — 'off-five' instead of 'office' is a funny accident that he delivers with total conviction. Works because it adds insult to injury: he's kicking Jim out and can't even do that right.

jokes.text: Harvey says 'Boobs' after everyone has left Michael's office.
jokes.setup: The Harvey bit appears to have concluded; Pam and Jim have left.
jokes.punchline: Alone, Harvey (Michael) says 'Boobs' — Michael continuing to enjoy his toy by himself with no audience.
jokes.explanation: Single-word tag that perfectly punctuates the scene. The comedy is in the implication: Michael, alone, is still playing with Harvey, and the first thing he says is 'Boobs.' Maximum economy (one word), maximum character revelation. A laugh that builds on the scene but transcends it. One of the episode's best single moments.

jokes.text: Kevin challenges whether the tax forms are a big deal, and Angela claps back: 'Is it a big deal? Is it, Kevin?'
jokes.setup: Angela announces the tax forms issue; Kevin seems dismissive or unaware of the stakes.
jokes.punchline: Angela's withering rhetorical question — 'Is it a big deal? Is it, Kevin?' — drips with contempt.
jokes.explanation: Classic Angela contempt delivery — her condescension toward Kevin is a reliable dynamic. Competent character comedy but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'Five of us transferred from Stamford. There's two of us left... It's like we're touring Willy Wonka's chocolate factory, and dropping off one by one. Well, guess what. I'm not falling in a chocolate river.'
jokes.setup: Andy reflects on the Stamford transfers being picked off one by one.
jokes.punchline: The Willy Wonka metaphor — employees eliminating themselves like Golden Ticket children — capped with 'I'm not falling in a chocolate river,' which is both determined and absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best confessional jokes. The Willy Wonka metaphor is surprisingly apt and original — the chocolate factory as a workplace where people disappear through their own foolishness is genuinely clever. 'I'm not falling in a chocolate river' has the cadence of a real motivational statement, which makes it funnier. Andy's self-seriousness sells it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight arrives late; Jim immediately says 'Hey, Dwight, pass the tardy sauce.'
jokes.setup: Dwight arrives late to a morning meeting.
jokes.punchline: 'Pass the tardy sauce' — a fake condiment name that calls out Dwight's lateness with weaponized casualness.
jokes.explanation: Jim's trademark casual prank energy — 'tardy sauce' is a nice wordplay construction. Brief and efficient. The fact that Michael has to be told to 'get it' undercuts it slightly, but the joke itself is solid.

jokes.text: Andy's elaborate pause before choosing Michael as his sales call partner — 'Oh, I don't know... Michael Scott.'
jokes.setup: Michael gives Andy first pick of sales partners; Andy pretends to deliberate.
jokes.punchline: The fake deliberation reveals Andy's entire strategy — he's flattering Michael by performing a 'difficult decision' that was never in doubt.
jokes.explanation: Very Andy — the performative deliberation is perfectly in character for someone who is always working an angle. The audience sees through it immediately, which is the point. Character integration is the strongest element here.

jokes.text: Andy sycophantically picks Michael first, calling him 'PhD. Doctor of sales.' Michael responds with layers of mutual complimenting that spirals into absurdity.
jokes.setup: Andy gets first pick for sales partners and takes an obvious, calculated approach.
jokes.punchline: The mutual compliment exchange ('That's very gracious of you.' 'Well, it is very gracious of you to accept.' 'Well, thank you, sir.') devolves into meaningless social performance.
jokes.explanation: Character-specific to both Andy (shameless flattery) and Michael (bottomless appetite for praise). The escalating politeness becomes its own punchline. Runs slightly long.

jokes.text: Phyllis says she'll pick Karen. Michael says 'our resident senior.' Phyllis replies: 'We're the same age.'
jokes.setup: Michael introduces Phyllis as 'our resident senior' to indicate seniority.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis flatly corrects him — 'We're the same age' — revealing Michael called her old.
jokes.explanation: Economy is excellent — four words deflate Michael's oblivious condescension. The humor comes from Michael being both insulting and clueless simultaneously. A reliable Office beat.

jokes.text: Stanley refuses to pick anyone, says 'Pass.' Michael insists. Stanley says 'I'll take the kid.' Ryan's talking head: 'I was his second choice, after pass.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is asked to pick a sales partner. He attempts to opt out entirely.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's confessional — 'I was his second choice, after pass' — is a perfect articulation of being the least-wanted option.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured two-beat joke. Stanley's 'Pass' establishes the scene; Ryan's deadpan confessional delivers the real punch. 'Second choice, after pass' is concise, self-deprecating, and perfectly calibrated. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I'm very flattered. I was his second choice, after Pass.'
jokes.setup: Stanley reluctantly chose Ryan as his sales partner after refusing to pick anyone.
jokes.punchline: Ryan, in confessional, dryly notes he came in second place to the option of not participating at all.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke. The construction — 'second choice, after Pass' — is tight, surprising, and self-deprecating in a way that's both funny and a little sad. Ryan treating 'Pass' as a competing candidate is a great comedic logic twist. Highly quotable, well-structured, and earns its 8 score. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example in its economy and unexpectedness.

jokes.text: Jim says he wants to trade Dwight as a partner. Dwight immediately offers to trade too. Jim says 'Dwight and I used to go on sales calls all the time. In fact, I have a picture to remember that time.'
jokes.setup: Both Jim and Dwight desperately try to trade away each other as partners.
jokes.punchline: Jim's framing of having 'a picture to remember that time' implies the shared experience is something to be mourned rather than celebrated.
jokes.explanation: Solid irony from Jim — treating a mundane sales call photo as a traumatic memory. Sets up the next beat nicely.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head staring at a photo of himself with Dwight: 'Oh, young Jim. There's just so much I need to warn you about.' Pause. 'And yet, tragically, I cannot.'
jokes.setup: Jim looks at an old photo of himself with Dwight — presumably from a sales call they took together.
jokes.punchline: Jim's theatrical, mournful 'There's just so much I need to warn you about... And yet, tragically, I cannot' treats a mundane workplace situation as a profound tragedy.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. The structure is impeccable: the setup ('so much I need to warn you about') creates the expectation of a profound confession, and then 'And yet, tragically, I cannot' punctuates it with theatrical resignation about something completely inconsequential. The pause between the two lines is load-bearing. Jim's deadpan delivery would make this land as one of the series' most quotable confessionals. The 'tragically' is doing enormous comedic work — pure economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight arrives with his car. Andy comments on shirts on hangers in the back seat. Michael asks 'He does your laundry?' Dwight says 'Long story.'
jokes.setup: The group heads to cars; Dwight's car has hanging shirts in the back, visible to everyone.
jokes.punchline: 'He does your laundry?' / 'Long story.' — the absurdity of the power dynamic between Michael and Dwight is exposed publicly.
jokes.explanation: Efficient exposition-as-comedy. The visual of hanging laundry in a car is funny; 'Long story' from Dwight encapsulates the absurd humiliation of his situation.

jokes.text: Michael announces the sales teams as Amazing Race archetypes: 'You guys are the retired marines. You guys are the mother/daughter. You guys are the gay couple. And we are the firefighter heroes.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to motivate the teams by framing the day as The Amazing Race.
jokes.punchline: Michael assigns each pair a reality TV stereotype, revealing both his TV obsession and his complete lack of self-awareness — and of course assigns himself the 'hero' archetype.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael worldbuilding through pop culture. Assigning himself 'firefighter heroes' is perfectly on-brand narcissism. The specificity of the archetypes (retired marines, mother/daughter) is what elevates it above a generic joke.

jokes.text: Phyllis asks if there's a prize for winning. Michael says 'Just bragging rights.' Phyllis: 'Then how is this Amazing Race?' Michael: 'It's just... brrrrr.'
jokes.setup: Michael has framed the day as The Amazing Race; Phyllis probes the metaphor logically.
jokes.punchline: Michael deflates completely under scrutiny, making a car-revving noise ('brrrrr') as a non-answer.
jokes.explanation: Phyllis's logical takedown of Michael's metaphor is a clean reverse — she becomes the straight man. Michael's 'brrrrr' as a literal non-answer is a great character beat. The audience has been waiting for someone to puncture this, and the non-verbal deflation is the perfect payoff.

jokes.text: Jim refuses to sit in the front seat of Dwight's car, insisting on sitting in the back. 'It's the safest part of a car. In the event of a crash, the driver always protects his side first.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight get in Dwight's car together; the question of seating arises.
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers a pseudo-scientific justification for sitting in the back, treating a normal car ride as a potential combat/survival situation.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's survivalist logic applied to mundane situations is a show staple, and this is a solid example. The reasoning is internally consistent (by Dwight's standards), which makes it funnier than random weirdness.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'Every success I've ever had, in my job, or with the lady folk, has come from my ability to slowly and painfully wear someone down.'
jokes.setup: Jim reveals his strategy for dealing with Dwight through Michael.
jokes.punchline: 'The lady folk' — Jim's breezy self-awareness that his romantic success method is essentially psychological attrition.
jokes.explanation: Jim's self-deprecating charm is on display. 'The lady folk' is an intentionally archaic phrase that undercuts any pretension. The implication that his romantic strategy is 'wearing someone down' is a dark-funny insight into his character.

jokes.text: Michael explains the Dwight laundry situation. Andy responds: 'Wow, that is a long story, but quite well told, Michael. I find it very interesting.'
jokes.setup: Jim had set up 'What's the deal with Dwight doing your laundry?' to plant seeds with Michael. Michael tells the story.
jokes.punchline: Andy's over-the-top flattery of the storytelling quality itself — 'quite well told, Michael' — is transparent sycophancy that Michael completely accepts.
jokes.explanation: Andy's fawning is consistent with his character and advances the plot, but isn't the sharpest joke in the episode. Works as part of the ongoing Andy-sycophancy running gag.

jokes.text: Andy offers his services as Michael's laundry folder: 'I used to work at Abercrombie. So... pretty good folder.'
jokes.setup: Andy is in full ingratiating mode, looking for any angle to cement his relationship with Michael.
jokes.punchline: Volunteering to fold Michael's laundry, citing Abercrombie employment as a credential, is an absurdly specific and desperate form of flattery.
jokes.explanation: The Abercrombie credential is a lovely specific detail — it's the kind of information that only a person desperately searching for relevance would deploy. Andy's quiet confidence in his own folding ability is also funny.

jokes.text: Michael and Andy drive into a beauty salon. Andy asks to take the lead on the pitch. Michael: 'Mind? Nothing would delight me more.'
jokes.setup: Andy has spent the whole car ride flattering Michael. Now he asks for a favor — to lead the pitch.
jokes.punchline: Michael's extravagant acceptance ('Nothing would delight me more') mirrors Andy's own sycophantic register, suggesting Michael has been charmed and is now performing enthusiasm back.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the mirroring — Andy's flattery has infected Michael's vocabulary. A nice structural payoff to the car ride bit, though understated.

jokes.text: Dwight insists Jim leave the car keys. Jim: 'You still do that thing?' Dwight, still insisting: 'Leave the keys.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight arrive at a client. Dwight makes an unusual demand.
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'You still do that thing?' implies a longstanding absurd habit; Dwight's unapologetic repetition of 'Leave the keys' confirms he has a paranoid/controlling reason and will not explain it.
jokes.explanation: The unexplained 'thing' is very funny — implying that Dwight has a rich tapestry of irrational demands Jim has catalogued over the years. The joke's economy is excellent: we don't need to know why Dwight wants the keys, and not knowing is funnier.

jokes.text: Andy to Michael in the car: 'It's like everyone has their own special skill. You know, just like the Super Friends. Except for Dwight, who's kind of more of a super dud.'
jokes.setup: Andy is complimenting the Scranton team to Michael, comparing them to superheroes.
jokes.punchline: 'Super dud' — a neat rhyming deflation of the Super Friends metaphor applied to Dwight.
jokes.explanation: A serviceable joke that functions primarily as plot exposition (Andy planting seeds against Dwight with Michael). 'Super dud' is a reasonable pun but not inspired.

jokes.text: Andy: 'He'd be a Super Friend, if there was a Super Friend whose super power was always being late. You know? Hawkman.'
jokes.setup: Andy is riffing on the Super Friends analogy, diminishing Dwight.
jokes.punchline: Invoking Hawkman as the superhero most associated with lateness is an absurd, specific non sequitur that makes no logical sense — and is funnier for it.
jokes.explanation: The Hawkman name-drop is brilliant in its arbitrariness. There is no logical reason Hawkman is the lateness superhero, which is exactly why it's funny. Andy delivers it with total conviction. Memorable and quotable.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'My plan is taking longer than I thought. But I don't give up easily. I have walked two marathons, so...'
jokes.setup: Jim explains his long-game strategy to manipulate Michael against Dwight.
jokes.punchline: 'I have walked two marathons, so...' — the non sequitur credential of walking (not running) two marathons as proof of perseverance, with the trailing 'so...' implying the logical conclusion is obvious.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specific word 'walked' — not ran, walked. Walking a marathon is technically possible but deeply uncool as an athletic credential. Jim's casual 'so...' implies this is an unassailable argument. The trailing ellipsis is essential. Highly quotable and economical.

jokes.text: Dwight insists Jim walk ahead of him. Jim: 'That still leaves a 30% chance I'll attack you from the front.' Dwight: 'Yeah, but it'll be easier to stop.'
jokes.setup: Dwight won't let anyone walk behind him — 'seven out of ten attacks are from the rear.'
jokes.punchline: Jim plays along with the paranoid logic, noting a front attack is still statistically possible. Dwight's earnest counter — 'it'll be easier to stop' — treats the threat as real and manageable.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured back-and-forth. Jim baiting Dwight with 'a 30% chance I'll attack you from the front' is an excellent logical trap, and Dwight's unironic contingency planning ('I can always block the blow') is perfect character work. The internal consistency of Dwight's paranoia makes this funnier than a simple weirdness joke.

jokes.text: Andy casually claims to have 'caught an 80-pound shark off Montauk' with 'a rifle from the crow's nest' of his dad's '42-foot Bayliner.'
jokes.setup: The client mentions a fish caught at Lake Wallenpaupack. Andy tries to one-up with an increasingly absurd fishing story.
jokes.punchline: 'Sniped it with a rifle from the crow's nest' — rifles are not fishing equipment; sniping a shark is not fishing. The casual delivery makes the absurdity land harder.
jokes.explanation: Andy's one-upmanship is a great character trait and this instance escalates beautifully. 'Sniped it with a rifle' is the key phrase — it casually converts fishing into hunting, and the passive specificity ('from the crow's nest') adds to the absurdity. Well-crafted escalation.

jokes.text: Andy undersells Dunder-Mifflin as 'just two rooms and a warehouse.' Michael interrupts to correct him: 'We trade on the New York Stock Exchange. Ever heard of it? It's in New York.'
jokes.setup: Andy deliberately undersells to create a contrast pitch. Michael can't help himself.
jokes.punchline: 'Ever heard of it? It's in New York.' — Michael condescendingly explains what the NYSE is to a business client, as if they wouldn't know. The parenthetical geography is the crowning absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Michael's inability to stay quiet during a pitch is perfect. The condescension of explaining what the NYSE is and where New York is, to a business client, is a great cringe beat. 'It's in New York' is the killer add-on — pure Michael overexplaining.

jokes.text: After Jim rescues the pitch, the client says 'I swear, this guy could sell paper to a tree.' Michael immediately interrupts: 'No. Stop it. Stop. Ow.'
jokes.setup: Jim smoothly recovers the pitch; the client compliments Jim warmly.
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'No. Stop it. Stop. Ow.' — he's so overwhelmed by vicarious pride/embarrassment that he physically reacts to the compliment, apparently hitting himself or the car.
jokes.explanation: Michael's physical reaction to a compliment is a nice visual/physical beat. The 'Ow' at the end suggests he hit himself in excitement, which is perfectly Michael. Character-specific and efficient.

jokes.text: After the pitch, Michael asks 'Do we even want that guy buying our paper?' Jim: 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: They've just closed a sale. Michael retrospectively second-guesses the client.
jokes.punchline: Jim's single-word 'Yes' — completely flat, no elaboration needed.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the joke is entirely in the single monosyllable. Jim's exasperation is implicit. Not a standout joke but functionally excellent.

jokes.text: Angela in confessional, speaking in code about Dwight: 'This friend of mine... let's call her Noelle... this gallant gentleman... we'll call him Curt.'
jokes.setup: Angela wants to share something about Dwight covering for her but doesn't want to reveal their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Angela's code names — 'Noelle' and 'Curt' — are transparently thin covers, and her use of 'gallant gentleman' is both romantic and hilariously formal. The audience knows immediately who she means.
jokes.explanation: Angela's attempt at discretion while clearly talking about herself and Dwight is very funny. 'Gallant gentleman' is great Angela vocabulary — formal, slightly archaic, and completely sincere. The obviousness of the code names is the joke. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Andy tells Michael he 'really Schruted it' and explains: 'It's just this thing people say around your office all the time. Like when you screw something up in a really irreversible way, you Schruted it. I don't know where it comes from, though.'
jokes.setup: Andy apologizes for blowing the sales call, then invents a workplace idiom on the spot to further undermine Dwight.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't know where it comes from, though.' — Andy fabricates that 'Schruted it' is a common Scranton phrase, playing dumb about its obvious origin.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The concept — weaponizing a person's name as a verb for catastrophic failure — is inspired. Andy's feigned ignorance of the origin ('I don't know where it comes from, though') is perfectly calibrated manipulation. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny as a concept, funny as a character beat for Andy, and 'Schruted it' itself is genuinely quotable as a phrase. High craft all around.

jokes.text: Stanley introduces Ryan to his client Julius as part of his pitch, then says 'I'm gonna let Ryan do a little pitch for you while I do my crossword puzzle.'
jokes.setup: Stanley has a warm relationship with his long-term client and clearly doesn't feel the need to work hard.
jokes.punchline: Announcing he'll do a crossword puzzle mid-sales call is a perfectly casual display of Stanley's legendary disengagement from work.
jokes.explanation: Almost perfect character integration — the crossword puzzle is Stanley's signature accessory of disengagement. Doing it during a sales call he arranged takes it to a new level. The casual announcement to the client's face is what makes it extraordinary.

jokes.text: Ryan's pitch begins. He says 'Hi.' Client says 'Hello, Ryan.' Ryan says 'Hi' again. Long pause. Another 'Hi.'
jokes.setup: Ryan has been put on the spot to deliver a sales pitch to serious clients.
jokes.punchline: Ryan freezes completely, saying 'Hi' multiple times with long gaps — his business school education failing him entirely in a real-world situation.
jokes.explanation: The escalating 'Hi...Hi...Hi' is a masterclass in cringe comedy. Ryan's complete collapse under minimal pressure exposes the gap between his self-image and reality — a core Ryan character theme. The pauses between each 'Hi' are the punchline. The client's later comparison to 'my niece. And she's six months old' confirms the read perfectly.

jokes.text: Client recaps Ryan's pitch: 'And you just said, "Hi. Hi. Hi."... You sounded like... My niece. And she's six months old.'
jokes.setup: Ryan has attempted to recover from his opening freeze, but the client has been unimpressed.
jokes.punchline: Comparing Ryan to a six-month-old is the devastating formal evaluation of his performance. The pause before 'My niece' and the afterthought '...And she's six months old' is structured perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The six-month-old comparison is a perfect closer to the Ryan freeze sequence. The structure — 'You sounded like... My niece. And she's six months old.' — with its two-beat reveal is excellent. The specificity of 'six months old' (not 'a baby,' not 'a toddler') makes it funnier. One of the episode's harder laughs.

jokes.text: Jim's pitch: holds up his phone to demonstrate a competitor on hold. Kelly picks up immediately: 'Oh my God, Jim, how are you?' Jim closes with his card: 'I never take vacations, I never get sick, and I don't celebrate any major holidays.'
jokes.setup: Jim argues that Dunder-Mifflin's customer service is its competitive advantage.
jokes.punchline: The competitor hold music as a live prop, followed by Kelly's immediately enthusiastic personal greeting — and Jim's card, which lists his anti-vacation/anti-holiday policy as a selling point.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed three-part joke. The hold music prop is clever stagecraft. Kelly's 'Oh my God, Jim, how are you?' demonstrates that Dunder-Mifflin service is almost TOO personal. And Jim's card — 'I don't celebrate any major holidays' — is the perfect escalation of the customer service commitment to the point of self-erasure. The joke works as comedy, character work (Kelly, Jim), and actually functions as a good sales argument. Multi-layered and well-crafted.

jokes.text: Jim calls Dunder Mifflin customer service to demonstrate responsiveness; Kelly answers immediately: 'Oh my God, Jim, how are you?'
jokes.setup: Jim calls Dunder Mifflin to demonstrate their superior customer service vs. the big company on hold.
jokes.punchline: Kelly answers immediately but then immediately makes it personal — 'Oh my God, Jim, how are you?' — which is exactly the kind of over-personal small-company service that is both a strength and a liability.
jokes.explanation: Kelly's immediate 'Oh my God, Jim, how are you?' simultaneously makes Jim's point (fast, personal service) and undermines it (too personal). It's a great double-edged joke that works for the plot and as a character joke about Kelly. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Karen's talking head after the client says Jim 'was hung up on Pam for such a long time': 'That's nice. You can pay me back later for the makeover.'
jokes.setup: A client casually mentions Jim was hung up on Pam for a long time right in front of Karen, his current girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Karen deflects the awkward revelation with wry sarcasm about the 'makeover' (the sales call), masking obvious discomfort with breezy comebacks.
jokes.explanation: Karen's deflection is a good character moment — her dry wit as a coping mechanism. The gap between what she says and what she feels is the comedy. The 'makeover' callback is clever. Rewatch value because we know how Jim/Pam plays out.

jokes.text: Karen's reaction after the client mentions Jim was hung up on Pam: 'That's nice.' followed by implied awkward silence.
jokes.setup: The client has just told Karen that Jim couldn't get over Pam.
jokes.punchline: Karen says 'That's nice.' — the most controlled, tight-lipped possible response to devastating information delivered in a social setting where she cannot react honestly.
jokes.explanation: 'That's nice.' is perfect in its compression. Two words contain hurt, forced composure, social performance, and dread. The economy is exceptional — what could be a long dramatic scene is compressed into two words that say everything. The Office at its best uses this kind of restrained delivery. Earns its 8 score.

jokes.text: Andy shows Michael a toll booth receipt from New York City as 'evidence' against Dwight. Michael: 'Why would Dwight go to New York without telling anyone?'
jokes.setup: Andy presents the receipt as damning evidence, implying Dwight went to see Jan.
jokes.punchline: Michael's guileless question — delivered as genuine confusion rather than accusation — shows he's already suspicious but can't quite close the loop himself. Andy has to lead him there.
jokes.explanation: Primarily a plot-advancing beat. The comedy is mild — Michael's slow processing is funny but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Fool me once, strike one. But fool me twice... strike three.'
jokes.setup: Michael is building to a proverb about Dwight's betrayal. He starts with 'Fool me once, strike one.'
jokes.punchline: The baseball metaphor collides with the proverb and produces something nonsensical: 'strike three' as the consequence of being fooled twice, skipping strike two entirely.
jokes.explanation: A genuine gem. Michael conflates two idioms — 'fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me' and baseball's three strikes — and produces something that sounds like wisdom but is logically broken. The ellipsis before 'strike three' implies he's considered this carefully. 'Strike two' goes unmentioned, which is the actual punchline hidden in plain sight. This is one of the most quotable Michael Scott lines — it works because it sounds almost correct. Exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head about Karen: 'I like Karen. She's pretty. Appears intelligent. Well, I like pretty women who have the appearance of intelligence.'
jokes.setup: Dwight gives his assessment of Karen.
jokes.punchline: 'Appears intelligent' — correcting 'intelligent' to 'appearance of intelligence' reveals Dwight's deep condescension toward women delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The self-correction from 'intelligent' to 'appearance of intelligence' is a genuinely sharp character moment. Dwight thinks he's complimenting Karen while revealing his own paternalism. The structure of correcting himself mid-sentence is well-crafted.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'My girlfriend is also beautiful and smart. She could be a model, or a college professor — which is intimidating to a lot of guys. We should go on a double date.' Karen: 'No, thank you.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just praised Karen; he pivots to talking about his own girlfriend (Angela).
jokes.punchline: Inviting Karen on a double date in the middle of a sales call, after an unsolicited girlfriend pitch — Karen's flat 'No, thank you' is the perfect response.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's social obliviousness produces this non sequitur double-date invitation. Karen's crisp 'No, thank you' is the perfect straight-man response. The joke is also secretly funny because Dwight can't reveal Angela is his girlfriend.

jokes.text: Dwight's name on the corporate security sign-in sheet: where it asks you to 'state your business,' Dwight wrote 'Beeswax Not Yours, Inc.'
jokes.setup: Andy discovers Dwight snuck to corporate and checks the sign-in sheet.
jokes.punchline: 'Beeswax Not Yours, Inc.' — Dwight's written response to a formal security question is a playground retort formatted as a corporation name.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a series highlight. 'Beeswax Not Yours, Inc.' is inspired — Dwight takes a childish 'mind your own beeswax' and formats it as a legitimate business entity, which both defies the form AND technically answers it. It's absurdist, character-specific, visually funny as a written prop, and extraordinarily quotable. The 'Inc.' is the killer detail — implying Dwight has incorporated his privacy concerns. Exceptional craft.

jokes.text: Confrontation: Michael demands to know what Dwight was doing. Dwight: 'I cannot tell you what I was doing there. But you have to trust me.' Michael pauses, then: 'That's what she said.' Dwight: 'Don't you dare.'
jokes.setup: Michael is in the middle of a serious confrontation about Dwight's loyalty. Michael sets up the classic opportunity: 'I want you to think about it long and hard.'
jokes.punchline: 'That's what she said' — Michael can't resist even in a serious moment. Dwight's furious 'Don't you dare' shows he sees it coming and is appalled by the timing.
jokes.explanation: The joke isn't just 'That's what she said' — it's that Michael uses it during a dramatic, emotionally charged confrontation, and Dwight's 'Don't you dare' (implying he heard the setup coming from a mile away) is the real joke. The timing subverting the serious scene is what earns this a higher score than a standard TWSS deployment.

jokes.text: Angela: 'I'll just stand up in front of the office, and reveal our true love. It won't be that bad. Look at Kelly and Ryan.' Dwight: 'I hate those two people more than anything in the entire world.'
jokes.setup: Angela suggests they just go public with their relationship to resolve the crisis.
jokes.punchline: Dwight using Kelly and Ryan as evidence of why they should NOT go public — while Angela used them as evidence they SHOULD — and his visceral hatred of them is perfectly Dwight.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's absolute contempt for Kelly and Ryan ('more than anything in the entire world') delivered in the middle of a tender moment is great character comedy. The irony that Angela used them as a positive example is the structural engine.

jokes.text: Karen's talking head: Jim admits he had a crush on Pam before leaving for Stamford. Karen: 'Did I ever have a thing for her? No. Why, did she say something?'
jokes.setup: Karen asks Jim directly if he had feelings for Pam. Jim denies it immediately.
jokes.punchline: Jim's instant 'No. Why, did she say something?' — the denial followed by a revealing follow-up question that proves the denial is false.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured. 'No. Why, did she say something?' is a perfect comedic construction — the denial and the betraying follow-up question in the same breath. It's funny as a joke, heartbreaking as character work, and rewatchable because we know everything Jim is hiding. Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Jim's confessional admitting he had a crush on Pam before leaving — 'I had... a crush on her... before I left. And I told her about it, and she didn't feel the same way.'
jokes.setup: Jim is in confessional mode, now being honest about his history with Pam.
jokes.punchline: The confession itself isn't a joke, but the understated way Jim refers to what was a major emotional event as simply 'a crush' — combined with the ellipsis pauses — is darkly funny in context. The understatement is the comedic layer over the drama.
jokes.explanation: More dramatic than comedic, but the understatement ('a crush') for something the audience knows was significant functions as Office-style tragicomedy. Not a big laugh moment but contributes to the episode's emotional texture.

jokes.text: Dwight's resignation speech: 'Although I love this company more than almost anything in the world, I have decided to step down from my post and spend more time with my family... I do not fear the unknown... we all shall fall.'
jokes.setup: Dwight stands before the office to make an announcement.
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers a grandiose resignation speech full of political-leader language — 'step down from my post,' 'I do not fear the unknown,' 'we all shall fall' — for a paper sales job.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's self-importance finding its ultimate expression — he speaks of resigning a sales job as if he's stepping down from the Roman Senate. 'We all shall fall' as a farewell to co-workers selling paper is perfectly absurd. Strong character integration; Dwight is the only character who would frame this with such gravity.

jokes.text: 'In other words, I'm quitting. So...'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just delivered a several-sentence grandiose resignation speech.
jokes.punchline: 'In other words, I'm quitting. So...' — Dwight deflates his own oratory with a bald declarative, followed by a trailing 'So...' as if awaiting applause.
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff to the grand speech. The joke is in the contrast — all that rhetoric reduced to 'I'm quitting. So...' — and the 'So...' implies Dwight expected a dramatic reaction and is waiting for it. The economy is exceptional. One of the episode's most satisfying single lines.

jokes.text: Dwight gives his belongings away during the exit, including a sequence of 'Just take it... Except this... Good luck... And this one. Oops.'
jokes.setup: Dwight begins distributing his belongings as part of his dramatic exit.
jokes.punchline: The sequence degrades from solemn ('Just take it') to accident ('Oops') — Dwight's grand gesture undermined by fumbling with his own props.
jokes.explanation: A decent physical beat that undercuts Dwight's dignity at a key moment. The 'Oops' lands because it's so tonally wrong for the moment he's constructing. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael's eulogy for Dwight: 'Not by me... so much. But he will be missed.'
jokes.setup: Michael says 'Dwight will be missed' — a sincere-sounding sentiment.
jokes.punchline: The qualification 'Not by me... so much' immediately undercuts it, revealing the statement was hollow — and the pause before 'so much' suggests Michael almost stopped himself.
jokes.explanation: The self-correction structure — sincerity immediately undermined — is a reliable Office joke but executed well here. 'Not by me... so much' has the rhythm of someone trying to be diplomatic and failing. Good economy.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Dwight... from sales... was one of the most honorable and efficient employees this company has ever had. One of my life goals was to die right here, in my desk chair. And today, that dream was shattered.'
jokes.setup: Michael continues his tribute to Dwight.
jokes.punchline: 'One of my life goals was to die right here, in my desk chair. And today, that dream was shattered.' — Michael pivots from honoring Dwight to mourning the death of his own fantasy of dying at his desk.
jokes.explanation: Michael's tribute devolving into a lament about his own shattered desk-death dream is wonderfully dark. The reveal that Michael had a specific fantasy about dying at his desk is both absurd and oddly poignant. The pivot from eulogizing Dwight to eulogizing his own life goal is classic Michael self-centeredness. Dark, specific, and character-rich.

jokes.text: Andy's final talking head: 'Am I happy about the way things turned out? Well, happy's such an ugly word... But I saw what needed to be done, and I did it. And now I'm thrilled. So it's pretty... Hello? Pretty good.'
jokes.setup: Andy reflects on having orchestrated Dwight's firing/resignation.
jokes.punchline: 'Happy's such an ugly word' — delivered with philosophical gravity — before Andy immediately says he's 'thrilled.' The phone interruption mid-sentence ('Hello? Pretty good') undercuts the confessional's self-importance.
jokes.explanation: Andy's faux-philosophy ('happy's such an ugly word') followed by immediately claiming to be thrilled is a good self-undermining joke. The phone call interruption mid-sentence is a nice comedic accident that makes the confessional feel spontaneous. 'Pretty good' as the deflated conclusion is well-timed.

tmdb_overview: Michael decided to send his employees out into the field for sales calls. He paired himself up with Andy. He let the veterans choose who they wanted their partners to be. Phyllis chose Karen, Stanley chose Ryan and that left Jim and Dwight paired together. This wasn't the first time Dwight and Jim had done sales calls together.
